course_description:
MSTU3150 is a course that explores recent approaches to the study of motion pictures as art. The course is designed to draw upon and build upon the gateway and cornerstone courses, as well as complement the capstone course, of the Film and Television major. We will explore the particular, formal qualities of motion pictures as well as the meanings and values of particular movements and works in conjunction with some recent publications from a broadly aesthetic perspective. The central aim of the course is to develop your capacity to make judgements about the films or television shows you watch; judgement, as we will discover, is central to the act of critical writing about them.

The main thing you will be learning and practicing is the articulation (to yourself and others) what you think, feel or otherwise know about movies. Central to this is the act of making a judgement. In part that means bringing into a legible form what we feel or think or want to say about something that matters to us. Knowing what matters, why it does and why that might matter, or ought to, to others is part of the learning and practicing. We will look at how film scholars have done this in their criticism about movies and bits of movies they think matter, and you will earn marks in the course by doing this yourself.

course_aims: This course aims to familiarise students with recent approaches, developed both within film/tv studies and philosophy of art, to the study of motion pictures as art. As such, one goal is to provide students with an understanding of film/tv studies as a discipline, its relation to scholarship in other disciplines. More specifically, the course strives to facilitate students' critical thinking and abstract reasoning about the nature and value of motion pictures. It also endeavors to bolster transferable critical thinking and communication skills via intensive discussion sessions and writing.

learning_outcomes.description: Understand the development and relationship of distinct disciplinary approaches to studying motion pictures as art.
Use the terms, concepts, and arguments of a particular scholarly approach to develop original claims and analyses.
Critically evaluate pieces of scholarly writing to demonstrate understanding of different perspectives and approaches and their potential merits, constraints, and flaws.
Demonstrate understanding of the fundamental attributes of and issues related to aesthetic criticism and evaluation and apply such understanding to set films.
Demonstrate capacity to produce original criticism and develop one’s own critical voice.

assessment_details.task_description: Your task in this assessment is to evaluate a short sequence of film from one of the movies shown in the first 5 weeks of the course by writing a piece of criticism about it. This sequence must be no more that 1 minute long (it can be shorter). Your evaluation must be informed by your studies during the course, including course readings and any wider reading that you have done. learning_activities.topic: Mid-Semester Break

WEEK ONE: CRITERIA AND CRITICISM This week introduces you to the course, and will consider one of the ways in which the evaluation of film (and many other arts) takes place, that is, through the insistence on medium specific criteria. We will explore what that means with reference to the film Don't Look Now . Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

WEEK ONE: CRITERIA AND CRITICISM The tutorial will engage with and practice some issues and aspects of the topic introduced in the lecture and readings mainly through close reading of one or two sequences from this week's film.

WEEK TWO: V F PERKINS AND THE LIMITS OF CRITICISM V. F. Perkins is a major figure in the development of film theory and criticism and this week will explore the ways his work offers an alternative to the criteria-based evaluation we looked at in the first week. Perkins's writing on Max Ophuls's Letter from an Unknown Woman remains some of the finest criticism (in a close reading mode) ever written and we will look at both carefully. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

WEEK TWO: V F PERKINS AND THE LIMITS OF CRITICISM The tutorial will engage with and practice some issues and aspects of the topic introduced in the lecture and readings mainly through close reading of one or two sequences from this week's film. This week is the first In-Class Written Evaluation. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04, L05

WEEK THREE: AESTHETIC EXPERIENCE AS THEME AND SPECTACLE - FIRST EXAMPLE We might argue that criticism is a kind of report of aesthetic experience and in the next two weeks we will look at movies which attempt in various ways to depict aesthetic experience as well as other kinds of artistic activity and consumption. Tom Ford was a notable fashion designer before directing movies and Nocturnal Animals is his adaptation of a novel by Austin Wright called Tony and Susan and it is the example we will look at closely in order to think about how showing something that at first sight seems emphatically 'inner' like aesthetic experience, has to conjure a range of 'outer' forms in order to be legible. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

WEEK THREE: AESTHETIC EXPERIENCE AS THEME AND SPECTACLE - FIRST EXAMPLE The tutorial will engage with and practice some issues and aspects of the topic introduced in the lecture and readings mainly through close reading of one or two sequences from this week's film. This week is the second In-Class Written Evaluation. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04, L05

WEEK FOUR: AESTHETIC EXPERIENCE AS THEME AND SPECTACLE - SECOND EXAMPLE Last week we saw how aesthetic experience can be recruited as an aspect of a film's plot and drama as well as its own aesthetic shape. Celine Sciamma's 2019 film Portrait of a Lady on Fire seems to go a step further by directly depicting the artist at work and entangling this with a romance plot. The result is a strange and compelling film that mixes together flows of feeling - for art, community, music, and love - in a way that insists on the primacy of beauty amidst discouraging social and historical conditions. In other words it is a film of significant ambition when it comes to the spectacle of art and beauty and aesthetics. To what extent is it successful? Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

WEEK FOUR: AESTHETIC EXPERIENCE AS THEME AND SPECTACLE - SECOND EXAMPLE The tutorial will engage with and practice some issues and aspects of the topic introduced in the lecture and readings mainly through close reading of one or two sequences from this week's film. This week is the third In-Class Written Evaluation. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05

WEEK FIVE: THE FIGURE OF THE ARTIST - FIRST EXAMPLE The history of art teaches us that one of the major topics that emerges is the role and nature of the artist - we might call it a modernist (although it predates modernism by centuries) gesture, that is to recruit the making and the medium of making as a theme in the artwork itself. Put more simply: what do we get and how do we evaluate those works which make artistic consciousness central? Paul Thomas Anderson's Phantom Thread is about a couturier named Reynolds Woodcock who seems at the height of success and is shown as a very controlling and exacting character. The plot of the film turns on the extent to which that control is, in many ways, out of his hands. As with Portrait of a Lady on Fire we will practice evaluating both this theme and the extent to which it is realised with wit, intelligence and dramatic force. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

WEEK FIVE: THE FIGURE OF THE ARTIST - FIRST EXAMPLE The tutorial will engage with and practice some issues and aspects of the topic introduced in the lecture and readings mainly through close reading of one or two sequences from this week's film. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04
WEEK SIX: READING WEEK NO CLASSES
WEEK SIX: READING WEEK NO CLASSES

WEEK SEVEN: THE FIGURE OF THE ARTIST - SECOND EXAMPLE David Cronenberg's Crimes of the Future seems similar to Phantom Thread in having its central character, Saul Tenser, as an artist - a maker of art. Unlike Woodcock, the art he makes is himself but - perhaps paradoxically - his control over it is minimal. This theme, of art as a kind of involuntary gift (or 'syndrome') has some pedigree in the world of humanities criticism - the gifted artist. We will consider how some of the central themes of authorship and its relationship to the social and political world (as well as the world of the audience, the consumers of it) is handled effectively in the film. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

WEEK SEVEN: THE FIGURE OF THE ARTIST - SECOND EXAMPLE The tutorial will engage with and practice some issues and aspects of the topic introduced in the lecture and readings mainly through close reading of one or two sequences from this week's film. This week is the fourth In-Class Written Evaluation. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04, L05

WEEK EIGHT: TONE, FRIENDSHIP AND VIOLENCE AS AESTHETIC FEATURES We have looked carefully so far in the course at complex and amorphous things like the artist-character, the spectacle of aesthetic experience, the distinction between criticism led by the authority of criteria or criticism that accrues its authority from a close reading of the film itself. But what about cinema's capacity to show, represent and capture other aspects of congealed human experience? Michael Cimino's The Deer Hunter is an attempt to get to grips with nature of friendship under extreme conditions: how successful do we think this is, what dramatic or artistic (rather than documentary) truth is there in its handling of friendship in the face of violence? Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

WEEK EIGHT: TONE, FRIENDSHIP AND VIOLENCE AS AESTHETIC FEATURES The tutorial will engage with and practice some issues and aspects of the topic introduced in the lecture and readings mainly through close reading of one or two sequences from this week's film. This week is the final In-Class Written Evaluation. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04, L05

WEEK NINE: VIOLENCE AS VALUE This week we continue our look at one of the most direct forms of aesthetic engagement - fictional violence. It is one of the most prominent and controversial ways in which film technique, style and methods of realistic or gratuitous depiction continues to be discussed. This week we look at the notorious example of Reservoir Dogs - even more so than The Deer Hunter this is a film that is self-conscious about its methods, themes and forms of address that entangle the viewer in impossible kinds of allegiance. To what extent is there a moral cost or price to be paid for our aesthetic involvement? Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

WEEK NINE: VIOLENCE AS VALUE The tutorial will engage with and practice some issues and aspects of the topic introduced in the lecture and readings mainly through close reading of one or two sequences from this week's film. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04, L05
WEEK TEN: PUBLIC HOLIDAY NO CLASSES
WEEK TEN: PUBLIC HOLIDAY NO CLASSES

WEEK ELEVEN: ACTING AND BULLSHIT The conceit of The Man Who Wasn't There is to present a central protagonist, Ed Crane, who seems utterly devoid of any desire, quite unlike the usual film noir protagonist. This passive figure provides us with a fine opportunity to consider the achievement and significance of acting as another primary form of engagement with evaluation. After all so much of our judgement - as this course has already demonstrated - is caught up in whether or not we find the performances in the films convincing, thrilling, engaging, successful, and so on. Who is responsible for the performance - the actor alone? the director? the script? the editing? our own history as consumers of art? Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

WEEK ELEVEN: ACTING AND BULLSHIT The tutorial will engage with and practice some issues and aspects of the topic introduced in the lecture and readings mainly through close reading of one or two sequences from this week's film. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04, L05

WEEK TWELVE: ACTING AND THE LEGACY OF ROBERT BRESSON Robert Bresson is one of the most revered film directors not least because his handling of actors (many of whom are non professional) is distinctive; we continue our interest in acting, performance and the handling of character interiority by looking at the ways Bressonian acting gets inherited in contemporary cinema. Among the closest to Bresson's style are the Belgian directors and brothers Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardenne and this week we will look at their 2019 film Young Ahmed and explore the ways it handles the depiction and avoidance of interiority. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

WEEK TWELVE: ACTING AND THE LEGACY OF ROBERT BRESSON The tutorial will engage with and practice some issues and aspects of the topic introduced in the lecture and readings mainly through close reading of one or two sequences from this week's film. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04, L05

WEEK THIRTEEN: AESTHETICS AND SPEED This week we look at one of defining medium-specific aspects of cinema, its depiction of movement, especially speed. In looking at one of the most visually dynamic films of the past decade ( Top Gun: Maverick ) we will pull together the various strands of the course: medium-specific criteria/close textual reading/aesthetics as spectacle/the figure of the artist/friendship/violence/interiority and acting as well as tone. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

WEEK THIRTEEN: AESTHETICS AND SPEED The tutorial will engage with and practice some issues and aspects of the topic introduced in the lecture and readings mainly through close reading of one or two sequences from this week's film. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04, L05

Course guidelines Communication Expectations While you are a student at UQ, all communication must be conducted according to the UQ Student Code of Conduct . The UQ Library has a helpful Communicate and collaborate online module . Email is the primary way for you to send messages to, and receive information from, the School and our staff. You must use your UQ email address (not a private address) to communicate with staff. You should add a clear subject line, including course code, and a 2-3 word statement. You can send email at any time, however, please do not expect responses outside normal working hours (Monday to Friday from ~8am to ~5pm). Emails that constitute bullying, harassment or discrimination against staff contravene the Student Code of Conduct. Emails like this will be reported to the University, and the matter will be pursued as misconduct. Learning activities
